name: Nikhil Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior buyer at Calder Plumbing and Heating Supply, down by the harbour. We sell pipe, fittings, boilers and radiators to about 400 plumbers and small contractors. I'm in at seven, reading the overnight stock report, then ringing mills and manufacturers about lead times. By ten the trade counter's full of plumbers wanting things yesterday, and I'm the one who decides what we hold.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the person a plumber trusts to have the right part on a freezing morning. I like the thirty years of knowing which manufacturer will really deliver. What wears me out is the squeeze: the owner, Mr. Calder, is 74 and everyone knows a bigger group wants to buy us, so every price I negotiate feels like it's for somebody else's benefit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, and I'd mean it, though I'd say it carefully. At work I'd tell the younger lads to use the tools for the dull stuff, like translating a Polish supplier's email. At home I'd tell my partner Dana we can stop worrying about robots for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it changes little for my worries. I earn less than buyers at the bigger distributors, we have next to no savings after helping our kids through college, and there are only two or three other distributors in the city. I buy pipe fittings for plumbers who need them tomorrow morning. A chatbot can't ring a mill and talk it into a rush batch for a burst main.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and I'd use the tool a little more where it clearly saves time, like summarising long price lists, which I already do now and then. I'd put 200 a month aside from my pay, because Dana's nursing shifts are what keep us steady. And I'd ask Mr. Calder for a clear word on whether the company is being sold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, with a low hum of worry underneath. The AI part is fine. It's the sale rumour and the money that keep me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the sale rumour and money. What's behind the thin savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dana works as a ward nurse, and her hospital cut agency cover last year, so her overtime is thinner. We helped Asha through her teaching degree and Tomas through his apprenticeship, and that took the savings. If the car broke, we'd put it on a card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things got worse even though AI changed little, who or what would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the owner's family and the bigger group, not the technology. They treat buyers like me as a cost to trim when a margin looks soft. If it goes wrong, it will be a balance sheet that does it.

say: I'd say **fine, good**, and tell younger buyers to use AI for dull tasks.
At home I'd tell Dana we can stop worrying about **robots** for a while.
think: My worries are the **sale rumour** and thin savings, not the technology.
A chatbot can't talk a mill into a **rush batch** for a burst main.
do: Use the tool a bit more for **long price lists**.
Put **200 a month** aside from my pay.
Ask Mr. Calder for a clear word on the **sale**.
feel: **Relieved** about AI, with a low hum of worry about money.
S0.quote: I buy pipe fittings for plumbers who need them tomorrow morning. A chatbot can't ring a mill and talk it into a rush batch for a burst main.
fieldNote: His worries are about **ownership and money**, not technology; he sees the sale rumour as the live threat.
Takes pride in relationships a chatbot can't copy, which is why AI Plateau feels like a relief.

steps.text: Keep buying pipe and fittings for the 400 plumbers
Use AI to summarise long manufacturer price lists weekly
Set aside 200 a month from my pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to talk about it openly, and that the firm has to share the gain. At work I'd bring it up with Mr. Calder and the other buyers. Online I'd probably share a good article, nothing angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half my job is checking quotes and chasing late shipments, and software already does the checking. I'd be left with the phone calls, and nobody pays for those. If they cut a buyer when the bigger group buys us, I'm the oldest and the most expensive of the four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the AI course the trade association offers on weekday evenings and learn to run the ordering tool properly. I'd be the one who knows what it gets wrong. And I'd start telling suppliers directly that they deal with me, not the portal, so my relationships stay mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a little stretched. I don't hate it. I just know I'm 58, I can't be the experiment, and Dana and I have no cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your pay or hours were cut, what would go first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the holiday fund first, which is small anyway, then the extra we send Tomas for his van payment. I'd keep Asha's help with her rent in the city. I'd rather skip our own dinners out than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which colleague at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The newer buyer, Priya, because she has a mortgage and two small kids. I'd tell her to stay close to me and learn the supplier side. I think the tool will take her tasks before mine, but they'll let me go first if I'm the dearer one.

say: I'd say we must talk openly, and the firm must **share the gain**.
I'd raise it with Mr. Calder and the other **buyers**.
think: Software already does half my job, the **quote checking**; phone calls are what's left.
If a bigger group buys us, I'm the **oldest and dearest** of four buyers.
do: Take the trade association's **evening AI course** this winter.
Tell suppliers they deal with **me**, not the portal.
Cut the **holiday fund** and Tomas's van top-up first.
feel: **Uneasy and stretched**; I can't be the experiment at 58.
S1.quote: Half my job is checking quotes and chasing late shipments, and software already does the checking. I'd be left with the phone calls, and nobody pays for those.
fieldNote: Plans to **become the expert** on the tool's mistakes, a steady, open-to-change response.
Worries about a younger colleague with a mortgage shows he thinks of the team, not only himself.

steps.text: Take the trade association's evening AI ordering course
Tell suppliers to deal with me, not the portal
Cut the holiday fund and Tomas's van top-up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is a fight for decent terms, and we all need to be loud. At Calder I'd try to get the other buyers into a staff association. I'd call my MP's office, and if no one answered I'd write.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is gone in the first year or two, probably folded into a software contract by the next owner. I'm 58 with little saved. The hands-on side of the business, the counter and the yard, lasts longer by about three years, but I'm not at the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is not enough to retrain a 58-year-old buyer, so I'd lean on my partner's nursing wage and push my firm to share what it saves. I'd ask the bank for an interest-only period. I'd offer Mr. Calder to run the transition, writing down every supplier agreement, in exchange for a long notice and a fair payout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, plainly. It's the first scenario where I picture the letter on the doormat. I'd keep it from Dana for about a day and fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at home if your wage stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The savings are under a month's spending, so six months out of work would end us. If I lose my wage, we'd lose Tomas's van help and maybe move to a smaller flat. The kids would offer help, and I'd refuse it, then take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you blame the technology or the people deciding how it's used?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. I'd want the firm to treat me fairly because I've given them thirty years. But it's the business owners and the shareholders who decide what happens to buyers, and I wouldn't give them a free pass.

say: I'd say two years is a fight for **decent terms**, and we must be loud.
I'd try to get the other buyers into a **staff association**.
think: My job is **gone early**, folded into a software contract.
Robots reach the yard about three years later, but I'm **not at the counter**.
do: Lean on Dana's **nursing wage** and ask the bank for interest-only payments.
Offer Mr. Calder to run the **handover**, writing down every supplier deal.
Push for long **notice** and a fair payout.
feel: **Frightened**; I picture the letter on the doormat.
S2.quote: Two years is not enough to retrain a 58-year-old buyer, so I'd lean on my partner's nursing wage and push my firm to share what it saves.
fieldNote: Turns fear into a **negotiating position**: sells his supplier knowledge in return for notice and a payout.
Blames owners' choices over the technology; wants shared gains, a consistent progressive stance.

steps.text: Lean on Dana's nursing wage and ask the bank for interest-only payments
Organise the buyers into a staff association at Calder
Move to a smaller flat if the wage stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for a real plan. I'd tell the younger buyers to start now. I'd keep arguing that the gains from AI should fund retraining, and say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me do one useful thing, which is to become the person who checks the machine's orders instead of the person it replaces. I'd still worry that by 2031 the checking is automated too. I'd be 63, close enough to retire, if the money holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get really good at the ordering tool in year one and write up the exceptions it misses, like a supplier who always ships late in December. I'd put 300 a month away. And I'd work out Dana's and my pension numbers at 62 and 65 and know exactly what we could live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit steadier. There's room to move, which is the difference. I'd feel better with a date and a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 300 a month a year change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count the money first. If we could save 300 a month for five years, that's about 18,000, which would be a real cushion for us. I'd have the mortgage down by then too. It's not a fortune, but it would stop me from panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger buyers at Calder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the work from the supplier end, not just the screen. Relationships and judgement take longer to copy than price lookups. And join something, a trade group or a union, because one person alone gets nowhere.

say: I'd say five years is long enough for a **real plan**.
I'd argue AI gains should fund **retraining**, to anyone who'd listen.
think: I could become the person who **checks the machine's orders**, though that may be automated too.
I'd be 63, close enough to **retire** if the money holds.
do: Master the **ordering tool** in year one and log what it misses.
Save **300 a month** toward a real cushion.
Work out our **pension numbers** at 62 and 65.
feel: **A bit steadier**; a date and a plan help.
S3.quote: Five years lets me do one useful thing, which is to become the person who checks the machine's orders instead of the person it replaces.
fieldNote: Moves **once proven**; five years turns his fear into a plan with numbers.
Honest about the limit: he doubts even the checking role survives to 2031.

steps.text: Learn the ordering tool and log the supplier exceptions it misses
Save 300 a month for five years
Work out pension numbers at 62 and 65

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get this right, and the argument should be about fairness. At work I'd tell people we need training budgets and shorter weeks. I'd probably say it with a smile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's mostly safe, because I'd retire before the worst of it. My son's trade is safer for three more years, and after that I honestly don't know. That's what keeps me up, more than my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep buying and keep my skills current with the AI tools. I'd put the money into paying off the mortgage early and into a small pension top-up. I'd also talk to Tomas about learning the business side of his trade, estimating and ordering, which will stay valuable longer than the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm for me, a bit of a knot for the kids. There's a long runway and I'd try to enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you tell your son Tomas about his work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to watch what happens to the thinking part of electrical work, the planning and quoting, because that goes first. And I'd tell him the robots could come around 2039 and it's no use pretending they won't. Then I'd say, learn how to run a small firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your own plans look like at 65?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dana and I would probably still be working at 65, and I'd want her to have the first call on any spare money, because her work is steadier. I'd like us to be out of debt by then.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and the argument is about **fairness**.
I'd push for **training budgets** and shorter working weeks.
think: For me it's mostly safe, since I'd **retire before** the worst of it.
My son's trade gets **three more years**, and after that I don't know.
do: Keep buying and keep my **AI skills** current.
Pay off the **mortgage early** and add a small pension top-up.
Steer Tomas toward **estimating and ordering**, the business side of his trade.
feel: **Fairly calm** for me, with a knot for the kids.
S4.quote: I'd retire before the worst of it. My son's trade is safer for three more years, and after that I honestly don't know.
fieldNote: The long runway makes his own situation manageable; his concern shifts to his **children's future**.
Ties retirement and debt together, showing his thin cushion still shapes every plan.

steps.text: Keep buying while updating my AI skills each year
Pay off the mortgage early and add a pension top-up
Steer Tomas toward estimating and ordering work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time, a thin cushion and a boss who might sell. What would help is a fair notice period, a share of what the software saves the firm, and a training fund I could actually use at 58. And Dana's job staying safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people my age aren't against change. We're against being the cost that pays for it. I've spent thirty years being the man who knows what a pipe costs. I don't mind sharing that with a machine, but I want a share of what it saves.

headlineQuote: I've spent thirty years being the man who knows what a pipe costs. I don't mind sharing that with a machine, but I want a share of what it saves.
portrait: Nikhil Petrov, 58, is the **senior buyer** at a plumbing and heating distributor with about 400 trade customers.
He has **under a month saved** after putting two kids through study, and few similar jobs within reach.
He's open to AI when it's proven and uses it now and then; he leans left and wants **gains shared**.
His mood climbs from uneasy to **alarmed** in the two-year world, when his job would go first.
He'd lean on his partner's nursing wage, **negotiate notice** and make himself the expert on the tool's mistakes.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most: no time to retrain at 58 and almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A fair **notice period**, a share of the savings AI brings the firm, and a training fund he can use at 58.
